fact: The U.S. EPA says the key to mold control is moisture control, that no type of mold grows without water or moisture, and that drying wet areas and items within 24 to 48 hours prevents mold growth.
quote: The key to mold control is moisture control. If mold is a problem in your home, you should clean up the mold promptly and fix the water problem. It is important to dry water-damaged areas and items within 24-48 hours to prevent mold growth. … There are many types of mold, and none of them will grow without water or moisture.
source_label: U.S. EPA, A Brief Guide to Mold, Moisture and Your Home (page updated Feb. 18, 2026)
notes: Read from the raw HTML with curl on 2026-09-25. EPA writes for homes; the page applies it outdoors only as far as the principle carries (no water, no mold).

fact: EPA says molds are part of the natural environment, that outdoors they break down dead organic matter such as fallen leaves, and that their spores float unseen through outdoor and indoor air.
quote: Molds are part of the natural environment. Outdoors, molds play a part in nature by breaking down dead organic matter such as fallen leaves and dead trees, but indoors, mold growth should be avoided. Molds reproduce by means of tiny spores; the spores are invisible to the naked eye and float through outdoor and indoor air.
source_label: U.S. EPA, A Brief Guide to Mold, Moisture and Your Home (page updated Feb. 18, 2026)

fact: EPA says molds produce allergens and irritants, and that inhaling or touching mold or its spores may cause hay-fever-type reactions such as sneezing, runny nose, red eyes and skin rash in sensitive people.
quote: Molds produce allergens (substances that can cause allergic reactions), irritants, and in some cases, potentially toxic substances (mycotoxins). Inhaling or touching mold or mold spores may cause allergic reactions in sensitive individuals. Allergic responses include hay fever-type symptoms, such as sneezing, runny nose, red eyes, and skin rash (dermatitis).
source_label: U.S. EPA, A Brief Guide to Mold, Moisture and Your Home (page updated Feb. 18, 2026)

fact: For homes, EPA advises keeping indoor relative humidity below 60 percent, ideally 30 to 50 percent, as part of mold prevention.
quote: Keep indoor humidity low. If possible, keep indoor humidity below 60 percent (ideally between 30 and 50 percent) relative humidity.
source_label: U.S. EPA, A Brief Guide to Mold, Moisture and Your Home (page updated Feb. 18, 2026)
notes: An indoor guideline. The page uses it only as a yardstick beside outdoor humidity readings and says so.

fact: At CoAgMET's Fort Collins station on the CSU campus, relative humidity stayed at or above 60% all day on 26 of 365 days in 2025, never more than 3 days in a row, and dropped below 60% at some point on every other day.
quote: fcl01 (Fort Collins, CSU Campus, elevation 4997 ft), daily QC data 2025-01-01 to 2025-12-31 (365 days): days with rhMin ≥ 0.60 = 26 · longest run of consecutive days with rhMin ≥ 0.60 = 3 · days with rhMin ≥ 0.70 = 16 · days with rhMin ≥ 0.80 = 9 · rhMin mean 0.284
source_label: CoAgMET (Colorado Climate Center) daily data, Fort Collins station (CSU campus), 2025
notes: Computed 2026-09-25 from the JSON at the source_url (rhMin = the day's minimum relative humidity, as a fraction; 365 of 365 days valid). Days at or above 0.60 by month: Jan 4, Feb 5, Mar 1, Apr 3, May 4, Jun 2, Jul 0, Aug 2, Sep 1, Oct 2, Nov 1, Dec 1. A research weather station in open air, not a shaded backyard corner. Same station and file as artificial-turf-static-shock.coagmet-fort-collins-rh-2025.

fact: At CoAgMET's Greeley 4 station, relative humidity stayed at or above 60% all day on 25 of 364 recorded days in 2025, never more than 4 days in a row, and dropped below 60% at some point on every other day.
quote: gly04 (Greeley 4, 1.5 mi N of Greeley Airport, elevation 4683 ft), daily QC data 2025-01-01 to 2025-12-31 (364 valid days): days with rhMin ≥ 0.60 = 25 · longest run of consecutive days with rhMin ≥ 0.60 = 4 · days with rhMin ≥ 0.70 = 15 · days with rhMin ≥ 0.80 = 7 · rhMin mean 0.276
source_label: CoAgMET (Colorado Climate Center) daily data, Greeley 4 station, 2025
notes: Computed 2026-09-25 from the JSON at the source_url; May 5, 2025 has no rhMin (-999) and is left out. Days at or above 0.60 by month: Jan 5, Feb 5, Mar 1, Apr 3, May 3, Jun 1, Jul 0, Aug 1, Sep 1, Oct 2, Nov 1, Dec 2. Same station and file as artificial-turf-static-shock.coagmet-greeley-rh-2025.

fact: The Colorado Climate Center says 70 to 80 percent of the plains' yearly precipitation falls from April through September, that widespread storms bring soaking moisture from early March through early June, and that winter more often brings dry air and strong winds.
quote: A very large proportion (70 to 80 percent of the annual total) falls during the growing season from April through September. Cool season precipitation can be important for soil moisture recharge, but midwinter precipitation is light and infrequent. More often, winter brings dry air and strong winds contributing to the aridity of the area. From early March through early June, periodic widespread storms bring soaking beneficial moisture that helps crops and grasslands.
source_label: Colorado Climate Center (Colorado State University), Climate of Colorado
notes: Section on the eastern plains, which includes the Northern Colorado Front Range towns.

fact: CSU Extension says algae on lawns is more common in thin, shaded, over-fertilized and over-watered turf than in well-drained turf, that compacted spots where water stands are especially susceptible, and that watering in late afternoon or early evening has been reported to increase it.
quote: This problem is more common in thin, shaded, over-fertilized, and over-watered turf than in well-drained, healthy turf. Compacted areas, especially where water stands, are especially susceptible. … Watering in late afternoon or early evening has been reported to increase problems with algae.
source_label: CSU Extension, PlantTalk Colorado 1558, Algae and Turfgrass
notes: About living lawns. The page uses it for the conditions algae favors (shade, standing water, evening wetting), not as a finding about synthetic turf.

fact: CSU Extension says gray snow mold, a fungus disease of Front Range lawns, develops under prolonged snow cover or where leaves and debris pile up over fall and winter, most often on north-facing and shaded lawns and where drifted or plowed snow is deep.
quote: Gray snow mold, caused by the fungus Typhula incarnate can occur on many Front Range lawns. Snow mold occurs during periods of prolonged snow cover, but can also occur where leaves and other debris have accumulated on lawns during the fall and winter. North-facing lawns, shaded lawns and areas where snowplowing or drifting snow created especially deep snow are most commonly affected. … The fungus is active in moist lawns at temperatures just above freezing.
source_label: CSU Extension, PlantTalk Colorado 1543, Gray Snow Mold in Lawns
notes: Species name spelled as the source spells it. A disease of living grass; the page uses it only for where snow and leaves keep a yard wettest.

fact: CSU Extension says lawn mushrooms sprout after prolonged wet weather where dead organic matter such as old tree roots, stumps or construction debris has accumulated, and that they should not be eaten by people or pets unless identified as edible.
quote: Mushrooms sprout in lawns after prolonged periods of wet weather, often in areas where dead organic matter has accumulated. Old tree roots, stumps or home construction debris, especially sawdust, encourage their growth. … Lawn mushrooms may be poisonous or may cause allergic reactions and should not be eaten by humans or pets unless proper identification shows they are edible.
source_label: CSU Extension, PlantTalk Colorado 1506, Mushrooms & Fairy Rings

fact: CSU Extension says foamy patches of slime mold on lawns or wood mulch are common in Colorado after warm, humid, rainy spells or fresh wood mulch, are more unsightly than harmful, and can be raked off once the area dries.
quote: The sudden appearance of “foamy” patches of slime mold on lawns or wood mulch is common in Colorado and can be disconcerting. Slime molds usually develop after rainy periods when temperatures are warm and humidity is high or the application of freshly-ground wood mulch. … The good news is that slime molds, a group of fast-growing, primitive fungi, are more unsightly than harmful and don’t cause any plant diseases. … If management is required for cosmetic reasons, decrease irrigation and rake the mulch to promote air drying. When lawns and wood mulch are dry, mow or rake the affected area to remove slime-mold.
source_label: CSU Extension, PlantTalk Colorado 1435, Slime Mold

fact: CSU Extension notes that artificial turf collects leaves and wind-blown dirt and debris that must be removed, and does not disinfect itself biologically the way a living lawn does.
quote: The companies that sell and install these lawns insist that they are virtually maintenance free, but artificial turf collects leaves and other wind-blown dirt and debris that must somehow be removed. Pet feces and urine deposits are problematic. These artificial surfaces do not naturally disinfect themselves by biological means like a living lawn does.
source_label: CSU Extension, PlantTalk Colorado 1537, Artificial Turf for Lawns
notes: The page's HTML splits "dirt" around an inline image ("dirt"); quoted as the rendered word. The same script quotes an installed-cost range that this page does not use.

fact: FieldTurf Landscape's care guide treats moss and algae as a problem of consistently damp, shaded areas, and advises good drainage with no standing water, more sun by trimming branches, clearing leaves and dirt so no rooting layer forms, and spot-treating with a 50/50 white vinegar and water spray scrubbed with a stiff brush and rinsed, or a turf-safe moss remover.
quote: Removing organic debris like leaves and dirt stops a top layer from forming where weeds or moss could take root. … Combating Moss, Algae, and Bacterial Growth in Damp Climates In consistently damp and shaded areas, like those found in Bellevue or Tacoma, moss or algae can sometimes appear. Improve Drainage: Ensure the area has good drainage and isn’t holding standing water. Increase Sunlight: If possible, trim back overhanging tree branches to allow more sunlight to reach the area. Use a Moss/Algae Treatment: You can use a 50/50 solution of white vinegar and water in a spray bottle to treat affected areas. Let it sit for a few minutes, then use a stiff brush to scrub the spot before rinsing thoroughly. There are also commercial, turf-safe moss removers available.
source_label: FieldTurf Landscape, Artificial Turf Maintenance Guide
notes: Read from the raw HTML with curl on 2026-09-25 (page dateModified 2026-09-05). A turf maker's care page. The two towns it names are in Washington State, not Colorado; the page does not repeat them.

fact: FieldTurf Landscape says quality foam pads are perforated so water drains through instead of pooling, that some have airflow channels underneath to prevent moisture buildup, and that turf laid directly on concrete can have water pool on top.
quote: High-quality foam pads have small holes throughout the material to allow drainage so water doesn’t pool. Tiny perforations can be present or horizontal slits/channels. Some pads feature vertical airflow channels on the bottom side to prevent moisture buildup underneath. … Since most foam pads have perforations throughout the material, they don’t retain water and allow it to drain through. This improves drainage compared to installing turf directly on a solid surface like concrete where water can pool on top.
source_label: FieldTurf Landscape, Foam Padding for Artificial Turf: Benefits, Uses & Safety
notes: Read from the raw HTML with curl on 2026-09-25 (page dateModified 2026-09-07). what-base-goes-under-artificial-turf.fieldturf-foam-pad quotes the same page.

fact: Synthetic Grass Warehouse's installer column says most putting green turf has no drainage holes in its backing, so moisture stays in the fibers where mold and moss can take over, that shade and moisture are the two causes, and that moss is worst in the cool weeks of spring and fall.
quote: Most putting green products are designed without drainage holes in the backing. … Since moisture has no place to go, it resides within the fibers. When this happens, mold and moss may take over the putting green surface, causing irregular ball roll. … There are two factors that cause moss in putting greens: shade and moisture. The majority of putting greens with moss that I have witnessed were all installed in shaded areas. Moss predominantly grows in climates where humidity and excessive moisture are present. Moss is more predominant during the cooler temperatures of early to mid-spring and during the fall months.
source_label: Synthetic Grass Warehouse, Ask JW: Moss and Putting Greens (published June 18, 2020; updated Dec. 29, 2022)
notes: Installer column from a turf distributor. Dates from the page's structured data.

fact: The same column removes moss by scraping with the blade held flat, scrubbing with a power broom or stiff broom while flushing with a hose, letting the turf dry and repeating as needed, then topping the infill back up, and says a green completely covered in moss may need to be replaced.
quote: Remove as much moss as possible from the surface. … Lay the blade of the scraper as flat as possible to prevent damaging the putting green’s surface. When most of the moss is removed, use a mechanical power broom to aggressively scrub the putting green fibers, removing any excess moss. If you do not own or cannot rent a power broom, a stiff asphalt broom with lots of elbow grease may do the trick. Remember that moss runs deep. Take a water hose, and flush the surface and power broom it at the same time. … Allow to dry. You may need to do this step multiple times to remove all the moss. … Sometimes putting greens completely covered by moss may need to be removed and replaced depending how bad they are. … When the moss is removed and the surface is dry, the turf infill will need to be replenished to the proper elevations.
source_label: Synthetic Grass Warehouse, Ask JW: Moss and Putting Greens (published June 18, 2020; updated Dec. 29, 2022)

fact: The same column recommends a coated infill carrying Microban, an antimicrobial it says fights mold and mildew, and notes that raw sand has no such built-in defense.
quote: Envirofill is equipped with “Microban”, an antimicrobial agent that fights mold and mildew. Raw sand does not have this built-in defense.
source_label: Synthetic Grass Warehouse, Ask JW: Moss and Putting Greens (published June 18, 2020; updated Dec. 29, 2022)
notes: A seller's recommendation of a product it sells; the page attributes it and names no brand.

fact: Synthetic Grass Warehouse's installer guidance says the lawn's valve should be capped or terminated so no water enters the old lines after turf goes in, and that existing irrigation should be capped at the valve and rerouted rather than capped head by head under the turf.
quote: If the natural grass is to be removed, then the grass valve must be capped and/or terminated to prevent any water entering the lines after the installation. … WHY CAN’T I JUST CAP THE EXISTING SPRINKLER HEADS? … I do not recommend capping sprinkler heads or leaving any irrigation under the turf system for many reasons. … So do the right thing. Cap the valve, terminate and re-route all existing irrigation, lines, and utilities that may cause issues during and after the installation.
notes: Read from the raw HTML with curl on 2026-09-25. sprinkler-system-after-artificial-turf.sgw-capped-heads-leak quotes the leak sentence from the same post.

fact: A turf-field engineer writes that organic infills hold moisture, that some naturally degrade and need replenishing every two to three years, and that organic infill can also grow weeds.
quote: However, because these fields hold moisture, they can be prone to freezing. … Some organic infill fields naturally degrade and need to be replenished every two to three years … Organic infill can also experience weed growth, requiring additional maintenance.
source_label: John M. Perry, P.E. (Gale Associates), Alternative Infills for Synthetic Turf Fields, Facilities Manager (APPA), January/February 2019
notes: Read with pdftotext on 2026-09-25. Sports-field context; the page uses it only for what organic infill does with water. artificial-turf-infill-types.gale-organic-moisture-freeze quotes the same article.
